Vula App Changes Public Health

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This is an uplifting, innovative tech-health story.

Unique Selling Point:
Imagine being a doctor in desperate need of expert advice, your patient is critical, and the specialist you’re trying to contact is not picking up the phone. South African Ophthalmologist Dr William Mapham experienced exactly this situation and decided that technology could change all that. His vision was that every healthcare worker has access to specialist advice at primary healthcare level through a medical app which he called Vula. Last year the Vula design team added an additional application totally focused on treating Covid-19 patients.

Summary:
Starting out in 2014 just for Ophthalmology, it now has 57 specialities on the app including cardiology; ear, nose and throat; burns; family medicine; HIV/Aids; and orthopaedics, and now a Covid-19 hub is making a massive impact. It also connects health care workers to free Covid-19 testing facilities, and because it’s all online the valuable research data on Covid-19 and all the variants is immediately accessible.
The Vula App has won many awards ¬¬- in 2019 it won the MTN Best Health App and this year was nominated by MIT SOLVE challenge as one of top 7 innovations submitted by 64 countries with 349 solutions in the 2021 Health Security & Pandemics category. The nomination recognised innovative approaches to equipping last-mile primary healthcare providers, strengthening disease surveillance, preventing the spread of misinformation, and combating the mental health impacts of disease outbreaks


Further information:
Quoting from a letter from a doctor at a specialist Covid hospital in Cape Town: “we accept Covid-positive management referrals from 13 major hospitals and emergency units across the Western Cape. Since its opening in July 2020 at the start of the pandemic in South Africa, we have had close to 6,500 admissions at our unit primarily managed though the Vula platform. With an average referral rate of between 60-70 referrals per day for one clinician to manage during our wave peaks, it would have been impossible to manage this without a simplified digital referral management solution. This allows my day and time to be manageable without getting bogged down with the volume of paperwork and lists at a desk all day.”
There are 4,000 doctors using the Vula app treating 19,000 patients a month, and within 11 seconds of a query being logged they get a response from a specialist. In the rural areas there is one doctor for every 18,500 people and 11 specialists to every 100,000 people in the country. Vula was designed with the input of specialists at Stellenbosch, UCT and Pretoria medical schools to assist the referral process by asking the right kinds of questions. Since its inception it’s cut down on unnecessary referrals by 31%, treating patients where they are. It’s also cut down on transport costs, mortality rates and the frustration and anxiety that both patients and doctors have to carry. Most importantly, it has reduced the burden on specialists who no longer have to sit on lengthy phone calls, spending hours writing up referrals. They are responding in real time, assisting, and treating many more patients.
The App allows for high-quality images, enabling specialists to give quality advice and it uses less data than WhatsApp. Urban poverty is often more extreme than rural poverty and the use of Vula in Khayelitsha and Mitchells Plain is dramatic. Overburdened clinics which invariably refer patients to tertiary facilities which have long waiting lists and limited beds, are having their burden alleviated by this immediate care via the app. Entire provinces’ health systems are being managed using the Vula App – it’s not only an application for individual health workers but administrators as well. With NHI around the corner, the Vula app could really come into its own, streamlining systems and creating access for public health patients.

Script:


Script: Catching an early morning wave before work was something Dr William Mapham could only dream of four years ago. At the time he was working a 16 hour day specializing in eye surgery, and developing a medical app at night- after 3 years of this gruelling schedule, his spine literally collapsed.
William” I wasn't able to walk for six months, and I used to take my zimmer frame down to the beach and I would watch the surfers. And I said one day, if I can walk again, I want to teach myself to surf.

Script “And without the support of his wife MA-RI-KE– a fashion designer, he wouldn’t be able to immerse himself in the next challenge - Mapham is the CEO of Vula mobile. An app designed to give immediate support to front line health care workers from public health specialists.
It all began 7 years ago, as a young doctor doing community service, in a remote hospital, and desperately needing specialist advice for his patients.
William: In 2018, I kind of had to make a choice. I said that to myself at once, Vula is seeing more patients daily that I saw in Swaziland, which was 80 a day, then maybe it's time for me to work on Vula full time ….- Vula are seeing a patient every minute now -it's really expanded beyond what I could do as a as one doctor.
Script: For example, let's say a frontline doctor was treating a burn victim. They select the closest hospital with a Vula burn specialist, select the burns page, fill in how extensive and severe the burns are, and the specialist on call now has the critical information to prescribe treatment. If they need to know more, they use the live chat function. And it’s as efficient in the 53 other areas of medicine, as it is in burns”.
Masa: typically, what is the ratio between patients and specialists?
William:, the ratio between patients and specialists does depend on the on the specialty. .. internal medicine, orthopaedics, there are more specialists ... And then if you go to the smaller specialties like dermatology, ophthalmology, rheumatology there, we don't have enough specialists at the moment. But the nice thing about Vula is, despite those scarce resources, we can maximize the use of those resources

Script: The beauty - is it’s designed in very close collaboration with specialists- something Mapham calls the IKEA effect, if you build it yourself, you value it more. All the most critical information is programmed in, and immediately available for the specialist to make a decision, on the next line of treatment

William: in a third of the cases, the frontline health care workers who are seeing patients don't have to refer the patient to a tertiary centre. The specialist can actually give them advice and they can treat the patients at their primary health care centre.

Clip 393 Link The Tygerberg hospital serves a population of 3.5 million people and is massively overburdened. In the past patients would just pitch up, but since using the Vula app it’s lessened the load for the various units using it
Script ‘Not only has it changed the lives of the referring doctors it has upsides for the specialists too - like orthopaedic surgeon Dr Etienne Joubert
Etienne 23:53:39:23 - you can now see which patients are emergencies that need to come straight away or if it's a patient that can be seen at our clinic on a planned date, or what one can also do through the app is to to tell the referring doctor what needs to be done.

Script: It’s reduced their patient load by 20%.

Dr Aderonke Ojewole is the registrar on call today and keeps an eye on the Vula app while working through the people attending the clinic

Ojewole Clip 330 00 20 46 23 50 year old male looks like a fracture by the ankle

Script: Dr Ojewole is giving advice to the referring clinic on this fracture – it needs surgery, but it’s not all bad news.

Ojewole” from what they tell me on the referral the soft tissues are fine, it looks like the patient can come on the following day for an admission …

Clip 301 01:19:36:13 Etienne: I think it's really made a difference for the patient as well, because if the patient's condition is not an emergency, they could end up spending a lot of time waiting in the emergency centre to be seen and then have to get back again.

Script: And when you are poor- that’s very expensive and if the hospital is a 4 to 7 hour drive away like in some Provinces, and 80% of the population is dependent on public health – it’s having a massive impact

Clip 348 Link: A phone ringing off the hook is one of the most stressful sounds, but for overworked medical staff and specialists they just don’t have the time to pick up the phone when the emergency in front of them is far more pressing
William “Once they click on the hospital they want to go it lists all the doctors that are on call right now , in the past you often spent 45 minutes trying to get through the hospital switchboard, getting the right doctor, and then you might not have the right information that specialist needed
Script: But with Vula, doctors aren't having to make phone calls, navigate switchboards, or page specialists to call back after theatre or ward rounds. When the COVID pandemic hit and the health care system was stretched to breaking point, they created a dedicated COVID page
Faried - it's a godsend….... The fact that you can have all that information at your fingertips ….with active feedback from the person that you were referring on the other side ...it simplifies the process
376 Clip Link: It’s so encouraging to see so all these empty hospitals beds but during the peak of the 3rd wave Dr Abdullah admitted 125 patients in one day, and thanks to the Vula app, by the time the patients arrived here all their vital information was already available
Script That information was uploaded by the referring doctors, ready for use by Dr Abdullah and his colleagues at Cape Town’s dedicated Covid hospital, Brackengate.
Faried: I think this pandemic has kind of proven that that,.., South African doctors are made of grit and steel and, …..nurses are made of courage ….they go way beyond the call of duty to ensure the people we look after are as best as we can

Script: And that dedication is reflected in the stats available on the app at the end of each month. Who took the most cases, how quickly they responded and where things fell apart

William 01:07:17:18 All the departments using Vula get all their stats from the previous month so they can see where all the referral patterns are happening. They can see where the workload is increasing or decreasing. The data is being used to motivate for extra posts in certain areas So I think the level above just the use of Vula by health care workers is actually by the health administrators so they can redesign the health care system almost in real time with data.

Script: The Western Cape Government has adopted it as its official referral platform, and its operating in 6 provinces, it's also spreading across Africa.
Clip 339 LINK: Dr Mapham’s heart has always been in public health and he has made enormous personal sacrifices to get the app where it is to today, never succumbing to the lucrative allure of the private sector - and it's paying off
William: And so there were times when I really wasn't really making any money, and so I wasn't really sure how to do that. -We've now got a company board. We've got a great team. We have a finance officer, so there's so much more support now than ever before. So I think if there's any kind of lesson I learned to ask for help and there are always people in the background too willing to give it

Script: And his team is spread around the country and unlike most tech environments Vula employs more women than men.

Masa: What's been the biggest reward for you?

William: I think the biggest reward for me is getting the feedback from the health care workers and getting a sense of how Vula helps them.
Faried: I can 100 per cent say that this this little gem of an app has been an absolute integral part, of our day to day fundamental mechanism here
